title: Recommend a book you loved
prompt: A classmate asks what book they should read next. Recommend one book and convince them to pick it up.
framework: Point: name the book and give your overall verdict
Reason: why THIS book suits them
Example: what happens in it (no spoilers) and what struck you most
Point: close with a direct recommendation
phrases: If you only read one book this year, make it...
What struck me most was...
It's the kind of book that...
Trust me, by the second chapter you'll be hooked.
I cannot recommend it highly enough.
nudges: What makes this book better than a similar one you did NOT enjoy?
Who would NOT enjoy this book? Being honest about that makes you sound credible.
checklist: I stated my main point in the first two sentences
I gave one concrete example, not vague praise
I ended by repeating the recommendation

title: Explain your hobby to a stranger
prompt: Explain your main hobby to someone who has never heard of it. Make them understand why you love it.
framework: Point: name the hobby and one-line summary
Reason: what you actually do, step by step
Example: one specific moment that captures why it's special
Point: invite them to try it
phrases: The best way to describe it is...
Basically, what you do is...
There's this moment when...
What keeps me coming back is...
You should come along once and see.
nudges: Which step would confuse a beginner most? Simplify your words there.
What does the hobby teach you that applies to other parts of life?
checklist: I avoided jargon, or explained each term I used
I described the process in a clear order
I shared one vivid personal moment

title: Talk about a mistake that taught you something
prompt: Describe a real mistake you made and what it taught you. Be honest — the value is in the lesson.
framework: Point: state the mistake plainly
Reason: how it happened, in sequence
Example: the exact moment you realised
Point: what you do differently now
phrases: To my regret, I...
At the time, I thought...
Looking back, the turning point was...
What I learned, above all, is...
Ever since, I always...
nudges: Was the lesson about skill, or about judgement? Say which.
Could someone else repeat this mistake? Warn them directly.
checklist: I described the mistake without blaming others
I showed the timeline clearly
The lesson is specific and actionable

title: Agree or disagree: homework should be halved
prompt: Take a clear position: should homework be reduced by half in schools? Defend your position.
framework: Point: state your position in one sentence
Reason: your strongest argument, explained
Example: evidence, experience or observation
Point: acknowledge the other side, then restate yours
phrases: My position on this is clear: ...
The strongest argument for this is...
Research from my own experience shows...
I understand why some people argue that... but...
On balance, I stand by...
nudges: State the OPPOSING argument fairly before knocking it down — that's how strong speakers argue.
What would change your mind? Saying that makes your position look reasoned, not stubborn.
checklist: My position is unambiguous
I presented the other side fairly
I gave concrete support, not just opinion

title: Convince your parents to let you take a trip
prompt: Persuade a cautious parent to let you join a week-long trip with friends. Address their real worries.
framework: Point: the request, stated clearly and respectfully
Reason: why this matters to you
Example: how you will handle money, safety and contact
Point: a concrete plan that answers their fears
phrases: I'd like to talk about something important to me.
I understand your concern about...
Here is my plan for that: ...
You can reach me anytime because...
I hope you'll trust me with this.
nudges: What is the parent's biggest unspoken fear? Name it before they do.
What compromise would you accept? Offering one shows maturity.
checklist: I addressed safety and money directly
My tone stayed respectful even while pushing
I ended with a clear, small ask

title: Describe a place that matters to you
prompt: Describe a place that is important to you so vividly that your listener can picture it.
framework: Point: name the place and its meaning in one line
Reason: what you see, hear and smell there
Example: one memory that happened there
Point: why you keep coming back
phrases: The first thing you notice is...
What makes it special isn't the view but...
Whenever I'm there, ...
It smells like / sounds like...
If I close my eyes I can still...
nudges: Use at least two senses beyond sight.
What small detail would only a regular visitor notice? That detail makes the description yours.
checklist: I used sensory details, not just visual ones
I included one specific memory
The meaning of the place is clear by the end

title: Explain why you admire someone
prompt: Talk about a person you admire (family, famous or fictional) and explain what makes them worth admiring.
framework: Point: who they are, in relation to you
Reason: the quality you admire most
Example: a moment that showed this quality
Point: how you try to copy it in your own life
phrases: The person I admire most is...
What sets them apart is...
There was this one time when...
Because of them, I try to...
Their influence shows up in how I...
nudges: Admire a quality, not just achievements — kindness beats medals in an explanation.
Where did you fall short of their example? Honesty strengthens the tribute.
checklist: I named ONE main quality, not a list
I gave a specific story, not a summary
I connected it to my own behaviour

title: Defend an unpopular opinion
prompt: Pick an opinion you hold that most people disagree with. Defend it calmly and logically.
framework: Point: the opinion, stated without apology
Reason: the logic behind it
Example: a case where it clearly holds
Point: what you are NOT claiming (limiting the argument)
phrases: I know this isn't a popular view, but...
My reasoning is simple: ...
Consider the case of...
I'm not saying... I'm only saying...
I can accept that reasonable people disagree.
nudges: The strongest defence is naming the argument's WEAK point yourself.
Swap 'everyone thinks' for 'many people think' — absolutes invite attack.
checklist: I stayed calm and logical, not defensive
I limited my claim to what I can actually defend
I acknowledged the mainstream view

title: Explain a trending topic to an elder
prompt: Explain something young people know well (a trend, app or phenomenon) to someone much older, without being condescending.
framework: Point: what it is, in one plain sentence
Reason: what people do with it, day to day
Example: a story of it in real use
Point: why it matters, or doesn't
phrases: The simplest way to put it is...
Think of it like..., but online.
For example, my friend uses it to...
It sounds trivial, but actually...
Whether it lasts is anyone's guess.
nudges: Find one comparison to something from THEIR generation — a bridge, not a lecture.
Where could this trend go wrong? Elders usually ask; answer first.
checklist: I used everyday words, no slang left unexplained
I compared it to something familiar
I respected both them and the trend

title: Tell someone their idea won't work
prompt: A friend is excited about a plan you believe will fail. Tell them honestly, without crushing their enthusiasm.
framework: Point: acknowledge the idea's real strengths first
Reason: the specific problem you see
Example: where the plan breaks down
Point: a suggestion or condition that keeps their dream alive
phrases: I love the energy behind this idea.
Can I be honest with you about one part?
My worry is that...
The numbers / timing just don't work because...
What if we adjusted it like this...
nudges: Critique the plan, not the person — pronouns matter: 'it' not 'you'.
Offer one genuine strength before the flaw; it buys your honesty a fair hearing.
checklist: I led with something true and positive
My criticism was specific, not general
I ended constructively

title: Introduce yourself to a new team
prompt: You're joining a new class, club or team. Introduce yourself in a way people remember.
framework: Point: name, plus one memorable label
Reason: what you bring, or what you're trying to get better at
Example: one quick, human detail
Point: an invitation to talk to you
phrases: I'm ..., and I'm the person who...
Most people know me for...
A random fact: ...
What I'm working on this year is...
Come find me if you want to talk about...
nudges: The best introductions include one small flaw or goal — pure confidence is forgettable.
Choose the ONE thing you want them to remember; cut the rest.
checklist: I gave one memorable label, not a list
I included one human detail
I ended with an invitation

title: Talk about a news event you care about
prompt: Explain a recent event or issue you care about, and why it deserves attention.
framework: Point: what happened, in one accurate sentence
Reason: why it matters beyond the headline
Example: who is affected, concretely
Point: what should happen next, in your view
phrases: The story, in brief, is this: ...
What the headlines miss is...
For the people affected, this means...
It matters because...
What I'd like to see happen is...
nudges: Separate the FACTS from your OPINION explicitly — listeners trust that distinction.
What is the strongest point on the other side? Mention it once.
checklist: I separated facts from my opinion
I said why it matters beyond the headline
I named one concrete effect on people

title: Say no without guilt
prompt: Someone you like asks for a big favour you can't give. Refuse kindly, clearly, and without over-apologising.
framework: Point: thank them, then the clear no
Reason: the honest, brief reason
Example: what you CAN offer instead
Point: end warm, door open
phrases: Thank you for thinking of me, but I can't.
The honest reason is...
What I can do is...
I hope it goes brilliantly.
Ask me again next time.
nudges: One 'sorry' maximum — stacking apologies makes a no sound negotiable.
Offering a smaller alternative shows care without surrendering.
checklist: I said the no clearly and early
I kept the reason brief and honest
I offered what I could instead

title: Pitch a solution to a daily annoyance
prompt: Pick something that annoys you every week (queue, traffic, mess, spam). Pitch a solution as if to a small investor.
framework: Point: the problem, one vivid sentence
Reason: who else suffers, how often
Example: your solution in action
Point: the first step to build it
phrases: Here's a problem we all pretend is normal: ...
Every single day, ...
My idea is simple: ...
Imagine instead...
Step one would be...
nudges: Quantify the annoyance — numbers make problems feel real.
Why hasn't this been solved already? Have an answer ready.
checklist: I described the problem vividly in one sentence
I quantified how many people it affects
I named the first concrete step

title: Retell a story from your childhood
prompt: Tell a true story from your childhood with a beginning, middle and end — make it worth hearing.
framework: Point: set the scene in two sentences
Reason: build up what was normal, then what changed
Example: the peak moment, slowed down
Point: the ending, and what it means now
phrases: I must have been about... years old.
Back then, our family...
Then one day, ...
I remember every second of what happened next.
Even now, whenever I..., I think of that day.
nudges: Slow DOWN at the key moment — pace is a storytelling tool.
One theme only: a story about everything is a story about nothing.
checklist: I set the scene in two sentences
I slowed down at the key moment
The story has one clear theme

title: Explain why you chose your path
prompt: Explain how you chose your course, job or direction — including the options you rejected.
framework: Point: where you are now
Reason: the options you had
Example: the moment or person that decided it
Point: no regrets, or what you'd change
phrases: People usually assume I chose this because...; actually...
At the time, my options were...
What tipped the balance was...
I sometimes wonder about the road not taken, but...
If I had to choose again, ...
nudges: Name the option you rejected and WHY — that's where your values show.
Avoid 'it just happened'; every path has a moment of decision.
checklist: I named the options I had
I described the moment that decided it
I said what I would change or keep

title: Calm someone down who is upset
prompt: A friend is panicking before results, an interview or a performance. Talk them down with words that actually help.
framework: Point: acknowledge the feeling first, no fixing
Reason: reflect their fear back in calmer words
Example: a time they handled something similar
Point: one small, immediate next step
phrases: It makes complete sense that you feel this way.
So the fear is that..., right?
Remember when you..., and it worked out?
Here's the one next thing: ...
Whatever happens, I'm here.
nudges: Order matters: feelings BEFORE solutions. Reversing it feels dismissive.
Offer one small step, not the whole staircase.
checklist: I acknowledged the feeling before advising
I recalled a similar moment they handled
I offered one small next step

title: Explain something complex simply
prompt: Pick something genuinely complex that you understand (a rule, a technology, a concept). Explain it in under a minute.
framework: Point: what it is, in one sentence a child could follow
Reason: how it works, using one everyday comparison
Example: where you see it in real life
Point: one sentence takeaway
phrases: At its core, it's just a way of...
It's like..., except...
You see this every time you...
The whole thing boils down to...
So if you remember one thing, remember...
nudges: Cut every term you can't replace with an everyday word — then explain the few that remain.
The comparison is the engine: test yours on one imaginary listener.
checklist: A child could follow my first sentence
My comparison explains how it works
I gave one everyday example

title: Ask for help without feeling small
prompt: You're stuck on something at work, school or home. Ask a specific person for help in a way that's easy to say yes to.
framework: Point: what you're stuck on, stated plainly
Reason: what you've already tried
Example: exactly what help you need, small and specific
Point: make it easy to decline
phrases: Could I borrow twenty minutes of your time?
I've tried..., but I'm stuck at...
What I need specifically is...
You're the best person to ask because...
If it's a bad time, just say so.
nudges: Asking for SPECIFIC small help gets better answers than general SOS.
Saying what you tried proves you're not offloading work.
checklist: I said exactly what I am stuck on
I mentioned what I already tried
My ask is small and specific

title: Talk about the future without clichés
prompt: Describe where you want to be in five years — without 'successful', 'happy' or other empty words.
framework: Point: one concrete picture of an ordinary Tuesday in that future
Reason: what you'll be able to do that you can't now
Example: the first milestone, within a year
Point: what you're willing to trade for it
phrases: Picture an ordinary Tuesday in 2031: ...
By then, I'll finally be able to...
The first milestone is..., which I can start this month.
To get there, I'm prepared to give up...
It's not a dream so much as a plan.
nudges: Concreteness is everything: a Tuesday beats a vision statement.
What are you giving up? Every future costs its present.
checklist: I painted one ordinary Tuesday
I named something I will be able to do
I said what I am willing to trade

title: Give feedback that lands
prompt: A teammate's work has a real weakness. Give feedback they can accept without feeling attacked.
framework: Point: what genuinely works in their work
Reason: the one thing that would most improve it
Example: a specific moment in the work
Point: a question that lets them save face
phrases: The strongest part is...
If I could change one thing, it would be...
Take paragraph three — what if...
What was your thinking behind...?
It's close; one more pass and it's there.
nudges: ONE improvement at a time; a list feels like a verdict.
End with a question, not a conclusion — it hands them the pen.
checklist: I led with what genuinely works
My improvement is specific and singular
I ended with a question, not a verdict

title: Explain a rule you disagree with
prompt: Name a rule (school, family, work, law) you think is wrong. Explain why — and what rule you'd put in its place.
framework: Point: the rule and your verdict
Reason: what the rule was meant to do
Example: where it fails or backfires
Point: your replacement, and its own risk
phrases: The rule exists to..., but in practice...
It fails whenever...
My alternative would be...
The trade-off is that...
No rule is perfect; the question is which failure you prefer.
nudges: Steelman the rule first: what problem was it actually solving?
Every replacement has a cost — naming it makes you a serious thinker.
checklist: I explained what the rule was for
I showed where it fails
My replacement has a named cost

title: Talk for one minute about nothing
prompt: Pick the most boring object near you. Speak about it for a full minute without stopping. The goal is flow, not wisdom.
framework: Point: name it and claim your territory
Reason: what it does, where it came from
Example: one memory or absurd detail
Point: a closing line, however small
phrases: At first glance it's just a..., but...
Someone designed this. Someone chose its colour.
It's been in my life longer than...
It will outlive me, probably.
And that's more than I ever expected to say about it.
nudges: The enemy is silence: keep talking, even into dead ends.
Absurd observations are allowed — enthusiasm beats accuracy here.
checklist: I kept talking without long pauses
I found something real to say about the object
I closed the minute deliberately

title: Apologise properly
prompt: You genuinely wronged someone. Apologise in a way that repairs, not defends.
framework: Point: name exactly what you did
Reason: acknowledge the impact on THEM
Example: what you'll do to prevent it
Point: no 'but', no excuses — just the ask
phrases: I want to apologise for specifically...
I can see it made you feel...
What I should have done is...
I've already changed...
I understand if you need time.
nudges: Kill the word 'but' — everything after it undoes the apology.
Describe the impact in THEIR terms, not your intentions.
checklist: I named exactly what I did
I described the impact on them, not my intent
I gave no excuses after the apology

title: Explain why a movie/show moved you
prompt: Talk about a film or show that genuinely affected you — and put your finger on WHY it worked.
framework: Point: the film and your honest one-line reaction
Reason: the specific scene or technique that got you
Example: describe that moment without spoiling the ending
Point: what it made you feel about your own life
phrases: I finished it and just sat there.
The scene that undid me was...
Without spoiling anything, there's a moment where...
What it's really about is...
It made me look at my own... differently.
nudges: Analyse the craft — naming the technique makes emotion sound intelligent.
One moment, described precisely, beats a whole plot summary.
checklist: I named the specific scene that moved me
I identified the technique that did it
I connected it to my own life

title: Defend a habit others find strange
prompt: You do something most people find odd (early waking, cold showers, writing nightly). Explain it so it sounds sane — because it is.
framework: Point: the habit, stated plainly
Reason: what problem it solves for you
Example: a before-and-after of your day
Point: what you'd tell someone starting it
phrases: I know how it sounds, but...
It started because I needed...
Before, my mornings were...; now they're...
If you tried it, start with...
The strange part is how normal it feels now.
nudges: Evidence from your own life beats research citations here.
Admit the cost; a habit with no downside sounds fake.
checklist: I stated the habit without embarrassment
I showed a before-and-after
I admitted one cost of the habit

title: Explain a memory you'd keep forever
prompt: If you could keep only one memory, which would it be — and why that one?
framework: Point: the memory, in one image
Reason: what it contains that nothing else does
Example: the moment itself, in detail
Point: what it says about what you value
phrases: If I had to choose, I'd keep...
It's not the most exciting memory, but...
Everything I needed was in that moment: ...
When I think of it, I can still...
I suppose it tells you that I value...
nudges: Small and specific beats grand — the ordinary reveals more.
The WHY is the real answer; the memory is just the vehicle.
checklist: I captured the memory in one image
I said what makes it irreplaceable
I named the value it reveals

title: Talk about money without awkwardness
prompt: Explain to a friend a money decision you made that they questioned — spending, saving or refusing to spend.
framework: Point: the decision, no embarrassment
Reason: the value behind it
Example: what you gave up and what you gained
Point: what you'd decide again
phrases: I know it looked strange when I...
The value behind it is...
What I gave up was...; what I got was...
Money is just..., and I needed...
I'd make the same call again.
nudges: State numbers where you can — vagueness creates the awkwardness.
Own the trade-off: every money choice buys something AND forgoes something.
checklist: I stated the decision without embarrassment
I named the value behind it
I owned the trade-off

title: Explain silence you regret
prompt: Think of a moment you should have spoken up and didn't. Explain what stopped you, and what it cost.
framework: Point: the moment, briefly
Reason: what exactly held you back
Example: what happened as a result
Point: what you'd do now, and what you've practised
phrases: The moment I keep replaying is...
I told myself it wasn't my place, but...
Afterwards, ...
What it cost me was...
Since then, I've...
nudges: Name the emotion that blocked you — fear, politeness, doubt? Precision here is power.
What's ONE sentence you could have said? Rehearse it; you'll need it again.
checklist: I described the moment honestly
I named the emotion that blocked me
I rehearsed the sentence I could have said

title: Make small talk that goes somewhere
prompt: Turn a dead-end small-talk exchange into a real conversation. Show the pivot, not just the opener.
framework: Point: respond to their statement, don't just answer it
Reason: ask one open question about something THEY care about
Example: share a small related thing about yourself
Point: let them talk — end with a question, not a statement
phrases: That's interesting — what made you pick that?
You mentioned...; how did that start?
Something similar happened to me: ...
So what's the story there?
I've wondered about that myself.
nudges: Answer AND ask: 'Yes — and what about you?' is the engine of conversation.
The pivot is from facts to feelings: 'What was that like?' beats 'Where was that?'
checklist: I responded, not just answered
I asked one open question about them
I ended with a question, not a statement
